sections.html:
Galveston sellers have three routes: a cash sale, a listing, or a sale without an agent. What the house is used for steers the choice, because the city holds a mix of residents, landlords and vacation rentals.

Owners occupy only 46.2 percent of units, so plenty of Galveston sellers hold rentals, second homes or inherited houses rather than a place they live in. Cash buyers can work around a tenant, a lapsed registration or a half-finished repair. Retail buyers seldom will, and their lenders may not either.

  • Cash sale: bought as-is, with a closing date you choose.
  • Listing: suits a house that shows well and can wait for a strong bid.
  • No-agent sale: you write the contract and handle disclosures.

Galveston leans toward renters, with moderate values and modest incomes. The population is about 53,636 and has held nearly flat since 2020. About 76.3 percent of residents lived at the same address a year earlier, which suggests steady rather than frantic turnover, so a motivated seller should not assume bidding wars.

Small households and one resident in five aged 65 or more point to downsizing and estate sales, which suit a seller who wants a simple closing.

Registration follows the house if it has ever been rented for short stays. The city requires every short-term rental to register annually and to carry a Galveston Vacation Rental number on every listing. Registration has been required since 2015, and the city itself now handles registration and hotel occupancy tax collection. Owners can register online or in person.

The fee is $250 for new registrations and renewals, due by December 31, with a separate number for each rentable unit. Registration asks for the property address or GCAD number, bedroom count, sleeping capacity and a 24-hour contact who lives within one hour of the rental. Failure to comply is a Class C misdemeanor with a fine not to exceed $500 per offense, and each day counts separately.

  • An unrenewed registration means platforms are told to remove your listing.
  • Tell the buyer whether the GVR number is active, so they know what is transferring.
  • If the house is no longer rented, email the city so it leaves the database.

The ordinance has been updated since it was first adopted. Read the current rules on the city's rental pages or call 409-797-3500 before you advertise the house as a rental. Anyone buying a house with a rental history should ask for the registration receipt and the listing history before closing.

sections.h2: Selling with tenants in the house
sections.html:
Leases ordinarily pass to the new owner, and a landlord may never lock a tenant out. To deliver the house empty, you need written notice and perhaps a court filing.

The steps run in sequence: written notice to vacate (three days if the lease sets no other period), a justice court filing with a hearing about one to three weeks later, a short appeal window, then a writ of possession carried out by an officer. Every step adds days your closing date must absorb.

Since renters are so common here, an all-cash investor who keeps the tenants is often the easiest way out. Put in writing how deposits and prepaid rent move to the buyer.

A lender generally cannot start foreclosure on a home loan until payments run more than 120 days late. Fixed notice periods follow, so the clock may be longer than you expect.

The default letter gives you a brief chance to catch up. The sale notice follows, posted at the courthouse and filed with the clerk several weeks before an auction on the first Tuesday of a month. That spacing is your time to find a buyer.

Closing ahead of auction day lets you pay off the loan yourself. Before you sign anything, ask the servicer for a payoff figure and whether a shortfall could remain.

sections.h2: What to gather before talking to buyers
sections.html:
Gather what the title company will ask for first. Missing paper holds up closings more often than repairs do, and a tidy file lets you compare bids on equal terms.

  • Your GCAD account number and the latest tax statement.
  • Payoff letters from every lender, including any home equity or second loan.
  • The GVR number, the latest registration receipt and any hotel occupancy tax records if the house was rented short term.
  • Current leases, deposit amounts and tenant contact details for any rented unit.
  • Any notice of default or notice of sale you have received, with its sale date.

With these in hand, you can ask a cash buyer for a written offer with a closing date, and you can ask a listing agent for a price range based on recent sales of similar houses. Compare the two by what you net after payoffs, taxes and recording, and get each figure confirmed in writing.

sections.h2: What a cash buyer will and will not do
sections.html:
An investor who pays cash can usually buy a Galveston house with a tenant, a lapsed rental registration, or an unfinished repair, because no lender is standing behind the deal asking for a clean file. That is the main reason owners of rentals and inherited houses end up here.

What a cash buyer will not do is ignore the price of those problems. Expect the bid to account for the tenant's lease, any back registration trouble and the cost of the work. Ask for the reasoning in writing, and ask whether the number changes after a walkthrough. Then compare it with a listing, remembering that a retail buyer's lender may insist on repairs or on a vacant house before approving the loan.

Whichever way you go, keep the closing date realistic. A buyer who offers a date far shorter than your title work allows is promising something nobody controls.

The Galveston Central Appraisal District (GCAD, at galvestoncad.org) values parcels, and the city's rental page sends owners there for their GCAD number. Values reflect January 1 ownership and condition, and bills arrive in the fall.

A bill still open after January 31 starts accruing penalty and interest the next day. Your deed gets filed at the clerk's office in the county that holds the parcel. Have the title company itemize payoffs, the tax split and recording charges ahead of closing, and keep the written breakdown with your records. If an error turns up on the statement, raise it before you sign rather than after funds move, because corrections are far harder afterward.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Galveston house that is a registered short-term rental?
faqs.a: Yes. Keep the registration current through December 31 each year and tell the buyer the GVR number and status so they can decide whether to keep renting.

faqs.q: Is the median value a price for my Galveston house?
faqs.a: No. The median owner-occupied value of $326,000 is a citywide figure, and your offer depends on the house and its condition.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Galveston house and keep the tenant?
faqs.a: Usually yes, since the lease passes to the buyer. A vacant house needs a notice to vacate and, if the tenant stays, a court case.

faqs.q: Does selling stop a Galveston foreclosure?
faqs.a: Often it does, provided closing happens before the auction date. Get a payoff letter and contact a title company early.

faqs.q: Where do I find my Galveston parcel's tax details?
faqs.a: Search galvestoncad.org by address or GCAD number, then ask the county tax office what is currently owed on the account.
